---
title: "Lecture 2 — Self-check answers"
sidebar: mfml
---

1. Estimate unknown \(f\) from paired data so we can predict; physics of \(f\) is often unavailable, so we use repeated observations + probability.  
2. Set \(\Omega\) of all possible outcomes of a chosen random experiment; **no**, it need not be numeric (e.g. \(\{H,T\}\)).  
3. e.g. single toss vs five tosses — different experiments → different \(\Omega\).  
4. The whole pipeline: illness / visit → imaging → digital image → clinician label (as one generative process whose outcomes we observe).  
5. To compare / quantify subsets (events); a bare set does not tell you “how much” or “how likely.”  
6. Non-negative; \(P(\Omega)=1\); \(P(\emptyset)=0\); additive on disjoint events; values in \([0,1]\).  
7. A subset of \(\Omega\) (in the collection \(\mathcal{F}\)) that we assign probability to.  
8. The math works with \(P\) as an abstract measure; human/clinical meaning is attached when you must make a real-world decision.
